title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #209
gist: A single week in early September 2026 stacked three world-model releases (Runway Solaris and GWM World 2, World Labs Atlas) plus OpenAI's Astra 6, Fervo's record 396 MW enhanced-geothermal PPA with Google, Tesla's Cybercab launch in Austin, the first robotically harvested iceberg lettuce, NASA's Roman telescope launching nine months early, and PSI's $58M raise for AI-driven physics. The connective thesis is that generative AI is escaping the text box into interactive pixels, atoms, and physics — and that all of it is bottlenecked on 24/7 power.

themes.theme: World Models Escape the Code Layer

insights.claim: Runway's Solaris is an 'Interface World Model' that generates a running application frame-by-frame in real time rather than having an LLM write code a browser renders, meaning the UI itself is generated pixels with no underlying codebase.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If apps can be generated as video rather than compiled code, the value of app frameworks, front-end tooling and even code-generation copilots gets partially disintermediated — watch inference cost per interactive frame as the gating variable.
insights.quote: Solaris generates the app itself, frame by frame, in real time, and when you click or drag something it generates the next frame. There is no code.
insights.locator: (1) World Model Week: Runway Solaris & GWM 2

insights.claim: World models are a distinct new class of foundation model that learn from watching the world and the actions taken in it, and can compute things that were previously uncomputable — a category separate from LLMs.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Treat world models as a separate investable model class from LLMs rather than a video-generation feature; the buyers (robotics, simulation, gaming, AV) differ from the LLM buyer.
insights.quote: these systems that learn from watching the world and the actions taken in it — are a fundamentally new kind of foundation model. They can compute what was previously uncomputable.
insights.locator: In March, General Intuition founder & CEO Pim DeWitte

insights.claim: The label 'world model' currently covers at least three technically different things — Runway's video models, World Labs' 3D reconstruction and generation models, and true action-conditioned simulators — and the September 2026 releases moved both companies toward the stricter definition.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Category confusion means comparable-sounding startups are solving different problems; underwrite on the input/output modality (video vs 3D vs interactive), not the marketing label.
insights.locator: There are a bunch of different kinds of models that are called World Models

insights.claim: World Labs' Atlas is an 'omni world model' trained from scratch jointly on text, images, video, camera poses, depth maps and 3D, generating up to a minute of 1440p video with pixel-perfect camera control driven by real camera geometry instead of text prompts like 'pan left'.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Geometry-conditioned control is what makes generative video usable in VFX, robotics sim and AV pipelines — it's the feature that turns a demo into a production tool.
insights.locator: Fei-Fei Li and the World Labs team showed off Atlas

insights.claim: Atlas will invent a coherent hallway between two unrelated photos when told they belong to the same building, and reconstructs real scenes into 3D from anywhere between one photo and a hundred.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Single-photo-to-3D collapses the capture cost of digital twins and real-estate/retail scanning, threatening incumbent photogrammetry and LiDAR-capture workflows.
insights.locator: it will invent a coherent hallway between two unrelated photos

insights.claim: Runway's GWM World 2 produces interactive real-time simulations as one continuous 720p 24fps video stream with 48000 Hz audio that responds to user input, shipping one day after its Solaris release.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Continuous interactive streams at 24fps mark the point where generated worlds compete with rendered game engines; watch for GPU-per-concurrent-user economics as the constraint.
insights.quote: generates full, interactive, real-time video simulations in one continuous 720p stream at 24 fps and audio at 48000 Hz, responding to your inputs as you explore.
insights.locator: And then, yesterday, Runway dropped another model - GWM World 2

insights.claim: OpenAI's Astra 6 launch triggered widespread claims that AGI has arrived, and Packy McCormick declines to endorse the AGI framing while calling it the most excited he has been to play with a new model.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Sentiment around a capability step-change tends to front-run measurable revenue; separate the 'AGI is here' narrative trade from actual enterprise adoption data.
insights.quote: A lot of people are saying AGI is here, and I don’t know exactly what that means
insights.locator: (1a) OpenAI Drops Astra 6

insights.claim: Matt Shumer's demo of Astra 6 building an Unreal Engine world populated by Astra-powered agents that coordinate to survive drew 4.43 million views, showing that multi-agent autonomous simulation is now a consumer-legible demo rather than a research artifact.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Agent-populated simulated environments are a plausible new demand driver for game-engine licensing and for long-horizon inference spend.
insights.locator: Matt Shumer, who built a simulated world full of Astra-powered agents

insights.claim: The near-term payoff of frontier models is delegation of work humans shouldn't be doing plus entirely new creative modes, rather than a discrete AGI threshold event.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Frames model progress as task-substitution economics — value accrues to whoever owns the workflow being delegated, not to the AGI label.
insights.quote: it does seem as if humans are going to be able to use these new models to do a lot of things for us that we shouldn’t be doing ourselves, and that it will let us be creative in entirely new ways
insights.locator: A lot of people are saying AGI is here

themes.theme: Enhanced Geothermal Lands Its Anchor Buyer

insights.claim: Fervo signed a 396 MW power purchase agreement with Google — the largest enhanced geothermal PPA ever signed by any company — to supply 24/7 carbon-free power to a potential Google data center in Utah from its Cape Station project in Beaver County starting in 2028.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A near-400 MW anchor offtake de-risks Cape Station's project finance and sets a public benchmark price point for the whole EGS category.
insights.locator: (2) Fervo Signs Its Largest Geothermal Deal Ever with Google

insights.claim: Google holds an option to take roughly 600 MW more from Fervo by June 2030, which would bring a single customer's total offtake to a full gigawatt.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The option is the real upside: a 1 GW single-customer contract would make Fervo's forward revenue largely a function of Google's exercise decision — a discrete, datable catalyst.
insights.locator: Google also gets an option to take roughly 600 MW more by June 2030

insights.claim: Enhanced geothermal's core unlock is that it uses shale drilling rigs to reach hot rock, so it no longer requires a hot spring or geyser — only heat within reach of a drill bit — which massively expands the number of viable sites.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Geothermal's addressable geography now scales with drilling capability, transferring shale-sector rig and completion expertise into clean baseload power.
insights.quote: enhanced geothermal uses shale drilling rigs to hit hot rock. You don’t need a hot spring or a geyser, just heat within reach of a drill bit, which is a lot more places.
insights.locator: if you’re new, enhanced geothermal uses shale drilling rigs

insights.claim: Fervo and Google have an escalating relationship history: Project Red in Nevada has powered Google data centers since 2023, and a 115 MW deal with NV Energy in 2024 invented the Clean Transition Tariff under which Google pays extra for more expensive clean power so other ratepayers don't absorb the cost.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The Clean Transition Tariff is a replicable regulatory template — its spread across states is the leading indicator for how fast hyperscaler-funded clean firm power can scale.
insights.locator: Project Red in Nevada has been powering Google's data centers there since 2023

insights.claim: Under Utah's SB132, Fervo may be able to sell power straight to Google's load, and the company frames the deal as adding around-the-clock capacity at no cost to existing ratepayers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Direct-to-load sales bypass the utility rate base — a structural change in who captures data center power margin, and a state-by-state legislative catalyst to track.
insights.quote: unlocks new, around-the-clock electricity capacity at no cost to existing ratepayers
insights.locator: under a Utah law called SB132

insights.claim: The escalating capability of world models, Astra-class models and whatever follows creates a direct causal pull on power demand, which is why frontier-AI news and geothermal offtake news belong in the same week's story.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The cleanest expression of the AI trade may be firm 24/7 generation contracted to hyperscalers rather than the model layer itself.
insights.quote: All of these models - World Models, Astras, whatever comes next - are going to need a lot of power.
insights.locator: Jennifer Hiller for WSJ

insights.claim: Tesla launched the Cybercab in Austin with public hailing via the Robotaxi app inside a geofence, using a purpose-built two-seat interior with butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or controls of any kind.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: First blank-sheet autonomous vehicle actually carrying paying public riders — the milestone that shifts Tesla's AV story from software promise to fleet operations.
insights.locator: (3) Tesla Launches Cybercab in Austin

insights.claim: The Cybercab specs out at nine cameras, a 48 kWh battery pack good for roughly 290 miles, a single 219 horsepower motor, 3,113 pounds curb weight, and Starlink in the roof.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A 48 kWh pack at 290 miles implies extreme efficiency and low BOM — the hardware basis for the sub-$30K build cost claim that underwrites robotaxi margins.
insights.locator: It has nine cameras, a 48 kWh battery pack

insights.claim: Elon Musk claims the Cybercab costs under $30,000 to build and about 20 cents a mile to operate at scale, with 10 cities by the end of 2026 and positive unit economics by mid-2027.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: These are falsifiable, dated targets — city count by year-end and unit-economics breakeven by mid-2027 are the two checkpoints to hold the robotaxi thesis against.
insights.locator: Elon says the Cybercab costs under $30,000 to build

insights.claim: Cost structure is the central AV differentiator: the Zoox is a roughly $250,000 minivan-shaped vehicle and Waymo pays Zeekr and Jaguar then bolts on about $100K of sensors, versus a claimed sub-$30,000 purpose-built Cybercab.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If the ~8x hardware cost gap holds, Waymo's operational lead can be eroded by capex per vehicle regardless of who has better autonomy today.
insights.locator: The Zoox is a $250,000-ish minivan-shaped thing

insights.claim: Waymo currently runs 500,000 paid rides a week across 14 cities on 4,000+ retrofitted Jaguars and Ojais, while Tesla's Texas fleet has only 45 Cybercabs alongside 269 Model Ys.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The scale gap is roughly two orders of magnitude today — near-term robotaxi revenue is Waymo's, and Tesla's case rests entirely on manufacturing ramp rate.
insights.locator: Waymo does 500,000 paid rides a week across 14 cities

insights.claim: Tesla intends to scale the Cybercab fleet partly by letting individuals sign up to purchase fleets of them, pushing vehicle capex off Tesla's balance sheet onto retail owner-operators.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A distributed-ownership model converts a capital-intensive fleet rollout into an asset-light network — materially different margin and financing profile than Waymo's owned fleet.
insights.locator: one way they want to scale is by letting people sign up to purchase fleets of them

insights.claim: Vehicle interiors are being redesigned as rooms rather than cockpits, a shift that went from the Zoox steering-wheel-free approval to Tesla's entertainment-oriented Cybercab in only seven weeks.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Opens a new supplier and media category — displays, audio, connectivity and in-transit content — as cabin time becomes monetizable attention.
insights.quote: basically a super comfortable lounge on wheels with a great TV and epic sound.
insights.locator: Back in Dose #204, when Zoox got the first US approval

themes.theme: Agricultural Robotics Clears the Harvest Barrier

insights.claim: Canadian startup Sami Robotics had a robot cut and pick a head of iceberg lettuce, described by practitioners as an 'AgTech moon landing moment' because harvest is the hardest part of agricultural automation and leafy greens are the hardest crop within it.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If leafy-green harvest is solvable, every easier crop follows — a signal to re-rate ag-robotics timelines and farm-labor cost assumptions.
insights.quote: I don't think people understand how monumental this kind of thing is. Harvest has always been the hardest part of agricultural automation and leafy greens are the hardest of the hard.
insights.locator: (4) Humanity’s First Robotically Harvested Head of Iceberg Lettuce

insights.claim: Leafy-green harvest resisted automation because every head is a different size, the cut must land in exactly the right spot without bruising, and skilled human crews with knives are already very fast — a combination of variable geometry, damage sensitivity and a high human baseline.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Explains why ag-robotics ROI hinges on beating an already-fast human benchmark, not just on technical feasibility — a useful screen for other manual-task automation bets.
insights.quote: Every head is a different size, you have to cut in exactly the right spot without bruising it, and a good crew of humans with knives is really fast as it is.
insights.locator: Every head is a different size

insights.claim: Reservoir VC runs an unusually narrow fund thesis of backing rugged AI startups that solve one high-value agricultural task then compound into adjacent industries, and backs it with a 40-acre Salinas farm operating as a robotics testing ground.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Physical test infrastructure as the differentiated VC value-add is a template for deep-tech funds — and a reason narrow ag-robotics theses can compound horizontally.
insights.quote: Reservoir VC invests in rugged AI startups that solve one high-value task in ag and then compound to adjacent industries.
insights.locator: As fund theses go, Reservoir VC’s might be the most specific

insights.claim: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on a Falcon Heavy from Pad 39A nine months ahead of schedule, which AstroForge founder Matt Gialich called unheard of for a billion-dollar-plus mission.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Schedule outperformance on a flagship science mission is evidence of a real management regime change at NASA — relevant to how aggressively to price future NASA program timelines.
insights.quote: 9 months ahead of schedule. That is unheard of for a billion-dollar-plus mission.
insights.locator: (5) NASA’s Roman Space Telescope Launches Nine Months Early

insights.claim: Roman carries the same 2.4 meter mirror aperture as Hubble — literally a spy satellite mirror the National Reconnaissance Office gave NASA in 2012 — but its Wide Field Instrument sees a patch of sky at least 100 times bigger than Hubble's infrared view at the same sharpness.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A 100x field-of-view gain at constant aperture is a survey-throughput step change, and a reminder that reusing existing defense hardware can compress science-mission cost.
insights.locator: Roman’s mirror is the same 2.4 meters as Hubble’s

insights.claim: Over five years Roman will survey more than two billion galaxies, measure how dark energy has stretched the universe over time, and run a microlensing census of planets toward the Milky Way's center from Sun-Earth L2 nearly a million miles away.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A defined five-year data firehose that will generate large-scale astronomical datasets — downstream demand for storage, compute and analysis pipelines.
insights.locator: Over five years, it’ll survey more than two billion galaxies

insights.claim: The proposed policy response to a rare on-time NASA success is to promote the responsible people and hand them another mission with performance-linked bonuses plus substantial authority — treating incentive design, not technology, as the binding constraint on space program execution.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If NASA institutionalizes performance-linked incentives under Isaacman, contractor selection and program schedules across the space supply chain get repriced.
insights.quote: Promote the people responsible and give them another worthy project with performance-linked bonuses and lots of authority and responsibility!
insights.locator: Casey Handmer, who’s been hilariously critical of his former employer NASA

insights.claim: Physical Superintelligence (PSI) raised $58 million to apply AI to fundamental physics, founded by Matthew Pines with Dr. Alex Wissner-Gross and Alex Klokus, on the premise that physics went down a wrong path decades ago and needs rescuing.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Venture capital is now funding fundamental-physics research directly as an AI application — a new frontier category distinct from applied AI SaaS.
insights.locator: (6) Physical Superintelligence Raises $58M to for Physics Takeoff

insights.claim: PSI spent 10 billion tokens in one week designing an interstellar mission that Starcloud's team had spent three months and one billion tokens on, producing a perihelion-pump maneuver that was then validated by NASA engineers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A concrete 10x-tokens-for-a-better-answer datapoint — evidence that inference scaling buys real engineering novelty, which supports sustained compute demand for R&D workloads.
insights.quote: In a week, they [PSI] spent 10 billion tokens on it, and it came up with this ingenious perihelion-pump maneuver that we then validated with the NASA guys.
insights.locator: We’d spent three months and one billion tokens on it

insights.claim: Starcloud CEO Philip Johnston announced The Fermi Explorer, a non-profit planning to launch a minimum viable spacecraft to Alpha Centauri departing in three years and arriving in roughly 80,000 years — explicitly expecting to be the first craft to leave for another star and the last to arrive.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The 'last to arrive' framing is an explicit bet that propulsion improves fast enough that later launches overtake earlier ones — a mental model for timing any long-duration capital deployment.
insights.quote: a minimum viable spacecraft to Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system, leaving in 3 years and arriving in around 80,000 years.
insights.locator: Yesterday, Starcloud CEO Philip Johnston announced a non-profit

insights.claim: Arena Physica released Heaviside-1, its second-generation foundation model for electromagnetism, which runs simulations in milliseconds that today's simulators take hours to complete.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Hours-to-milliseconds on EM simulation threatens incumbent EDA and physics-solver vendors while making iterative PCB and RF design a real-time activity.
insights.locator: our friends at Arena Physica

insights.claim: Arena Physica's electromagnetic model has been packaged into a free consumer-accessible Fields Studio app that lets anyone explore electromagnetic behavior around PCB designs, indicating physics-model distribution is going bottom-up rather than through enterprise sales.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Free bottom-up distribution of a physics foundation model is the same GTM that displaced legacy dev tools — watch for the same pattern eroding incumbent simulation licenses.
insights.locator: You can play with it yourself in the Fields Simulator here

themes.theme: Veil of Ignorance as Progress Argument

insights.claim: The strongest pro-progress artifact would be a 'Counterfactual Machine' that simulates a world with specific technologies removed and lets people experience it in VR, making the value of technology viscerally felt rather than argued.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Identifies an unbuilt product category — experiential counterfactuals — with obvious application to policy persuasion and education markets.
insights.locator: (Early Bonus) Any Human Ever

insights.claim: A site that randomly draws a life from the over 100 billion people who have ever lived demonstrates that most lives ever lived were Asian, poor and brief, operationalizing Rawls' Veil of Ignorance as a concrete argument that the present is the best time to be born.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A rhetorical framework for underwriting long-run progress optimism — useful for calibrating base rates against declinist narratives that dominate media flow.
insights.quote: most lives ever lived were Asian, poor, and brief
insights.locator: Someone built a site that lets you draw a life at random
